summary: This unit teaches you to report on financial activity: plan the month-end timetable, apply cut-off, accruals and prepayments, check the data, prepare the main statements and a profit-and-cash picture, calculate and explain variances, forecast the year-end outturn, report on working capital and capital spending, suggest options to improve performance, and present, review and correct reports honestly for boards, funders and parent ministries.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. **Reporting on financial activity** means turning the records of a business, a department, a charity or a public body into regular reports that show how it is doing against its plan, and what needs action.

Finance officers and managers in Jamaican firms, hotels, schools, charities and government agencies prepare these reports every month, quarter and year for boards, department heads, funders and parent ministries. A good report is **accurate**, **on time**, **compared with something useful** (budget, last year), **explained** and **clear about what must be done**.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in practice
rows: Plan and run the month-end process
Follow a timetable; apply cut-off; post accruals and prepayments; reconcile balances; check the trial balance.
Income statement, statement of financial position and cash position, and explain the link between profit and cash.
Actual against budget and last year, for the month and year to date, with causes and actions.
Project the full-year result from year-to-date actuals and known changes.
Report on working capital and capital spending
Receivables, payables, stock, cash; capital items and depreciation.
Set out effect, cost, risk and timing of each option.
Structure, charts, executive summary, sign-off, confidentiality.
Report honestly, correct errors openly, and resist pressure to make results look better.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** of scenario questions with sums (accruals, prepayments, variances, depreciation, exchange rates, percentages).
A **written paper** with short answers (terms such as accrual, prepayment, cut-off, trial balance, window dressing) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Practical tasks** done in a group: a monthly financial report prepared from a trial balance and budget, with adjustments, variances and commentary; and a variance investigation, outturn forecast and options presented at a management meeting.

blocks.note: Work every sum twice, and say whether a variance is favourable or adverse, and whether a percentage is of the budget or of the actual. The usual base is the budget.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Purpose, users and the month-end timetable

blocks.p: The main purpose of a monthly financial report to management is to **show results against plan and what needs action**. It is not a list of every transaction, a tax return, or a replacement for the year-end financial statements.

head: User
Needs
rows: Key results, profit and cash against budget, risks, decisions needed
Detail on their own areas: income, costs, variances, causes
Spending against the agreed grant budget, with explanations
Parent ministry or finance ministry (public bodies)
Report in the format and timing set by the ministry and the public finance rules
Profit, cash, debt cover and key ratios
Statutory returns; separate from management reports

blocks.p: The board gets **key results**; managers get **detail on their areas**. Giving everyone the full ledger helps nobody.
A timetable lists the tasks, the person responsible and the deadline in working days, so each task is done in order and reports are on time. Typical order:

flow: Cut-off: stop posting transactions for the month at an agreed time
Post and check sales, purchases, payroll and cash
Post accruals, prepayments, depreciation and other adjustments
Reconcile the bank, customer and supplier balances and stock
Run and check the trial balance
Prepare the statements and variance analysis; write the commentary
Review and sign-off by a senior finance person
Issue the report; follow up actions

blocks.note: If managers say the report is too long and arrives too late, ask them what they need, shorten the report and find the slowest steps in month-end. Do not add more tables, send it less often without asking, or tell them to read it more carefully.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Cut-off, accruals, prepayments and other adjustments

blocks.p: Accounts are meant to show the costs and income that **belong to the period**, whether or not the invoice has arrived or cash has been paid. This is the **accruals basis**. The adjustments below make that happen.

**Cut-off** is the rule that each transaction is recorded in the period in which it belongs. Goods worth J$350,000 that arrived and were used on 30 June, with the supplier's invoice arriving on 5 July, belong to **June**: record the cost in June as an accrued expense. Do not wait for payment, or the invoice date, or split it between the months.

An **accrual** is a cost that belongs to the period but has not been invoiced or paid. It is added to the accounts. If December's electricity bill has not arrived and usage is estimated at J$85,000, **accrue J$85,000** as December's cost. Estimate from meter readings or usage; when the real bill arrives, correct the difference.
A **prepayment** is a payment made in advance for a cost that belongs to a later period. The part that relates to a later period is carried forward as an asset, not an expense.

ul: A company with a year ending 31 March pays J$1,200,000 on 1 January for 12 months' insurance. Three months fall in the year: 1,200,000 x 3/12 = **J$300,000 expense**, and J$900,000 is a prepayment.
A company pays J$600,000 on 1 October for 12 months of security. Year end 31 December: three months used, nine months ahead. Prepayment = 600,000 x 9/12 = **J$450,000**.
A year ending 31 March, J$360,000 paid on 1 February for 12 months of software: two months used (J$60,000), prepayment of 10 months = **J$300,000**.

head: Item
Effect on profit
rows: Prepayment (when the whole payment was recorded as an expense)
Increases profit (part of the cost removed)
Reduces profit for this period (carried forward as a liability)

ul: **Stock write-down:** goods damaged beyond sale (for example by flooding) are written down to what they can be sold for; the loss is reported as a cost. Do not leave them in stock at cost, move them to next year or add them to fixed assets.

**Depreciation** spreads the cost of a long-lasting asset over its useful life. Straight-line: (cost - residual value) / years. A van costing J$6,000,000, five years, no residual value: J$1,200,000 a year, **J$100,000 a month**.
**Foreign currency:** a US$ debt is restated at the current rate. US$20,000 owed when the rate moves from J$155 to J$158: 20,000 x 3 = **J$60,000 more** to pay, a cost.
**Bad debts:** make a provision for amounts unlikely to be paid.
**Reconcile** the bank, customer (receivables) and supplier (payables) balances to the ledger, so balances are complete and correct. Do not do it to make profit look higher or to reduce GCT.

The **trial balance** lists all ledger account balances to check that debits equal credits before reports are prepared. If you export figures to a spreadsheet, check that its totals agree with the system's trial balance.

blocks.p: Use the **same accounting policies** each month as in the year-end accounts, so that results can be compared and no surprises arise. Financial reporting in Jamaica for most companies follows International Financial Reporting Standards, adopted by the accountancy body; your organisation's accounting manual sets the local detail.

blocks.note: Never adjust figures just to improve the picture. Holding back invoices, not recording accruals or overstating stock is **window dressing**, and is dishonest.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: The statements: profit, cash and financial position

head: Statement
What it shows
rows: Whether the business made a profit or a loss over a period: income less expenses
Assets, liabilities and equity at a date
Cash flow statement or cash report
Cash received and paid out, and the bank balance
Amounts owed by customers, by how long outstanding

blocks.p: Profit matches income earned with the cost of earning it, whether or not cash has moved. Cash shows what was received and paid. A company can report a good profit and still see its bank balance fall, because:

ul: customers owe more (receivables rose);
cash was spent on stock, equipment or loan repayments;
costs were prepaid;
profit includes non-cash items such as depreciation.

blocks.p: Report **both**, and explain the gap. Example: a business starts the month with J$2,500,000 in the bank, receives J$8,400,000 and pays out J$9,100,000. Closing balance = 2,500,000 + 8,400,000 - 9,100,000 = **J$1,800,000**. A guest house starts with J$1,200,000, receives J$5,600,000 and pays J$6,100,000: closing J$700,000.

blocks.note: GCT collected from customers is owed to the government. It is not part of income and should not be counted in profit.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: **Capital spending** (on long-lasting assets such as vehicles, buildings and machinery) is reported separately from **operating spending**, because capital items last for years, are approved and tracked as such, and are written off over time through depreciation. Operating spending goes straight to the income statement.
**Variance = actual - budget.** A variance is **favourable** if it improves profit and **adverse** if it reduces profit. Costs above budget and income below budget are adverse.
A total sales variance can be split into **volume** and **price**.

ul: **Volume variance** = (actual units - budget units) x budget price.
**Price variance** = (actual price - budget price) x actual units.
Another example: budget 5,000 units at J$800; actual 5,400 at J$780. Price variance = (780 - 800) x 5,400 = **J$108,000 adverse**.

blocks.p: Set a **threshold**, such as any variance over 5% or J$100,000. Travel budgeted at J$1,800,000 and actual J$1,926,000 is J$126,000 over (7%): explain it. Stationery J$12,000 over (4%) does not need a comment.

flow: Check that the figures are correct (no posting errors, correct period)
Ask the budget holder what happened
Identify the cause in specific terms (a price, a volume, a one-off, a timing difference)
State whether it is permanent or will reverse
State the effect on the year and the action planned

head: Weak explanation
Strong explanation
rows: 'Costs were higher than budget this month.'
'Overtime rose J$240,000 to cover two vacant posts, which will be filled in March.'
'Maintenance work planned for May will be done in July: a J$600,000 timing difference that reverses in July.'
'Fuel was about 19% over budget because of a 12% price rise and 6% more kilometres.'

blocks.p: A favourable variance that arises only because work has been delayed is a **timing difference**, not a permanent saving. It should not be spent on other things, and the forecast must include the later cost. Sales up 10% on budget but gross profit down: investigate **purchase prices, discounts and sales mix**.
Where a variance has several causes, split it. Administration costs J$900,000 over budget: show the overspend **by cost line and by cause**, not a single total.

The **outturn** is the expected full-year result. Start from checked year-to-date actuals. Forecast each remaining month line by line: rent and other steady costs continue; seasonal income follows its pattern; known one-off items (an annual licence, a pay rise from a given month) are added. For steady spending, a quick estimate is year-to-date / months elapsed x 12.

ul: After nine months a department has spent J$27,000,000 of a J$40,000,000 budget at a steady rate: 27,000,000 / 9 x 12 = **J$36,000,000**.
After six months J$15,000,000 at a steady rate: J$30,000,000 for the year.

blocks.p: State your **assumptions** and update the forecast each month. Report the forecast against the budget and say what is being done about any gap.

blocks.note: Percent of what? A variance is normally shown as a percentage of the **budget**. Always check which base the question uses.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Working capital, performance options and reporting for others

blocks.p: **Working capital** is the money tied up in stock and amounts owed by customers, less amounts owed to suppliers. Report each part monthly.

ul: **Receivables:** total owed, receivable (debtor) days = receivables / credit sales x 365, and an **aged debtors** analysis. If J$1,200,000 of J$8,000,000 owed is over 90 days old, that is 15%: chase these debts and review credit terms.
**Payables:** show amounts owed by age, so payments can be planned and late fees and supply problems avoided.
**Stock:** stock days = stock / cost of sales x 365, slow-moving and damaged items.
**Cash:** the bank balance and a short forecast.

blocks.p: When results fall short, present **options**, not only the problem. A hotel's food cost is 42% of food sales against a target of 35%: look first at portion control, waste, purchase prices and menu prices. Do not close the restaurant, move the costs to another department or cut housekeeping staff.

head: Option
Effect (J$)
Cost
Risk
Timing
rows: Raise selling prices on low-margin lines

blocks.p: Show each option's **effect, cost, risk and timing**, and **recommend one**. A list of ideas with no figures is not enough.

blocks.h: Reporting to funders and public bodies

ul: **Funders:** spending against the agreed grant budget, explained; not the charity's total spending on all its programmes, or only the unspent balance.
**Public sector bodies:** follow the parent ministry's requirements and the public finance rules for content and timing; not a private firm's format or what suppliers would like to see.
Keep **records** that support each figure.

head: Measure
Formula
Example
rows: Food cost 42% means gross margin on food of 58%

sections.title: Presenting, reviewing and acting with integrity

flow: Summary (one page): key messages, profit and cash against budget, risks, decisions needed
Key results table: month and year to date; actual, budget, last year
Variances over the threshold, with causes

blocks.p: Avoid putting the detailed tables first or leaving the summary to the end. At the board meeting, focus on **key messages, risks and the decisions needed**; do not read every figure aloud, use heavy technical language or avoid questions.

ul: To compare monthly sales with budget across the year, use a **line or column chart of actual and budget by month**. A pie chart of one year's total is not a comparison across time.
Label axes and units; do not truncate axes to exaggerate.
Use the same layout every month.

blocks.p: A **senior finance person** should check and sign the report before it goes to the board: figures agree with the trial balance, adjustments are right, commentary fits the figures. Do not let a report out unreviewed, or review it by someone with no knowledge.

If you find after issue that a J$450,000 invoice was posted twice, tell your manager, correct it and **send a note of the change**. Do not say nothing and quietly correct it next month, ask readers to destroy copies, or take the same amount off another line to balance it.

Boards, lenders, funders and the tax authority rely on your reports. If a senior manager asks you to hold back invoices so that profit looks better, **refuse, explain the rules and raise it as the organisation's policy directs** (your manager, the audit committee, the board). Doing it because the manager is senior, or promising to correct it later, is not acceptable. Professional accountants are bound by a code of ethics: integrity, objectivity, confidentiality and professional behaviour.

Share sensitive drafts, such as a planned branch closure that staff have not yet been told about, **only with those entitled to see them, marked confidential**. Do not leave copies in the staff room, email them to all staff or post them on social media.

After the board agrees actions to deal with an overspend, the next month's report should include **progress on the agreed actions and their financial effect**. Do not leave out the overspend, remove the commentary or remove the overspent line from a new budget.

blocks.note: Check one thing before you send any report: do the totals agree with the trial balance? If not, stop and find out why.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: explain the purpose of a monthly report and tailor reports to different users.
follow a month-end timetable, apply cut-off and post accruals and prepayments correctly.
calculate straight-line depreciation and the effect of an exchange-rate change.
write down damaged stock and reconcile balances to the trial balance.
explain the income statement, the statement of financial position and the difference between profit and cash.
calculate variances, state whether they are favourable or adverse, and work out percentages.
split a sales variance into volume and price.
set a threshold, investigate and explain variances, and separate timing from permanent differences.
forecast the year-end outturn and state assumptions.
report on receivables, payables, stock and cash, and compute receivable days.
set out options with effect, cost, risk and timing and recommend one.
present, review and sign off a report, correct errors openly and act with integrity.

terms: The rule that each transaction is recorded in the period in which it belongs.
A cost that belongs to the period but has not yet been invoiced or paid, added to the period's accounts.
A payment made in advance for a cost that belongs to a later period.
The list of all ledger account balances, used to check that debits equal credits.
Spreading the cost of a long-lasting asset over its useful life.
The difference between actual and budget; adverse if worse than budget, favourable if better.
The level of a variance above which an explanation is required.
A variance that arises because something happens in a different period and will reverse.
Money tied up in stock and amounts owed by customers, less amounts owed to suppliers.
The list of amounts owed by customers, sorted by how long each has been outstanding.
Improperly adjusting figures at a period end so that results look better than they are.
The short summary at the start of a report.
Spending on long-lasting assets such as buildings and machinery.

c1.title: Year-end adjustments at a Negril guest house
c1.text: A guest house in Negril has a financial year ending 30 June. Its profit before adjustments is J$2,500,000. On 1 March it paid J$480,000 for 12 months of vehicle insurance and recorded the whole amount as an expense. At 30 June, the rent for June (J$150,000) has not been paid or invoiced, and linen worth J$210,000 was delivered and used on 29 June but the supplier's invoice arrives on 4 July.

c2.title: A bakery's sales variances
c2.text: A Spanish Town bakery budgeted to sell 20,000 loaves in a quarter at J$300 each. It actually sold 22,000 loaves at J$280 each. The finance officer, Mr Andre Stewart, must report on sales and explain variances over the bakery's threshold of 5% or J$100,000. Fuel was budgeted at J$900,000 and actual fuel was J$960,000. Wages were budgeted at J$3,000,000 and actual wages were J$3,090,000.

c3.title: Profit but a falling bank balance
c3.text: A Spanish Town distributor reports a profit of J$6,000,000 for the year, yet its bank balance has fallen. The bank balance was J$900,000 at the start. During the year it received J$12,600,000 and paid out J$13,900,000. Amounts owed by customers rose from J$4,200,000 to J$7,800,000, of which J$1,560,000 is more than 90 days old. Credit sales for the year were J$54,750,000.

c4.title: Capital items and foreign currency
c4.text: A Montego Bay manufacturer buys a generator for J$3,600,000, with an expected life of six years and no value at the end. It also owes a US supplier US$12,000, payable next month. When the debt was recorded the rate was J$157 to US$1; now it is J$161. A fire has damaged stock which cost J$250,000 and which cannot now be sold.

c5.title: An outturn forecast at a hardware company
c5.text: A Mandeville hardware company has a full-year cost budget of J$38,000,000. After eight months, actual costs are J$24,000,000 and are running steadily month by month. An annual licence fee of J$600,000 is due in month 10 and is not yet in the figures. Maintenance of J$500,000, planned for month 4, was delayed to month 11.

questions.q: How much of the J$480,000 insurance is a prepayment at 30 June?
questions.why: The insurance started on 1 March, so four months (March to June) have been used: 480,000 x 4/12 = 160,000. The other eight months are prepaid: 480,000 x 8/12 = J$320,000.

questions.q: What should be done with the unpaid June rent of J$150,000?
o: Leave it until July, when it will be paid
Record it as a prepayment for July
Record it as an accrued expense for June
Ignore it, because no invoice has been received
questions.why: The rent is a June cost. Under the accruals basis it belongs to the year to 30 June whether or not it has been invoiced or paid.

questions.q: The linen delivered and used on 29 June has not yet been invoiced. What is the right treatment?
o: Include the cost in July, when the invoice arrives
Include the J$210,000 cost in the year to 30 June
Include half in June and half in July
Do not include it until it has been paid
questions.why: Cut-off puts the cost in the period in which the goods were received and used, which is June, regardless of the invoice date.

questions.q: What is the guest house's adjusted profit?
questions.why: 2,500,000 + 320,000 (prepayment removes part of the insurance expense) - 150,000 (rent accrued) - 210,000 (linen accrued) = 2,460,000. Check: net adjustment = +320,000 - 360,000 = -40,000.

questions.q: What is the total sales variance for the quarter?
questions.why: Budget: 20,000 x 300 = 6,000,000. Actual: 22,000 x 280 = 6,160,000. Actual is higher, so J$160,000 favourable.

questions.q: What is the sales volume variance, valued at the budget price?
questions.why: (22,000 - 20,000) x J$300 = J$600,000. More loaves sold than budgeted is favourable.

questions.q: What is the sales price variance?
questions.why: (280 - 300) x 22,000 = -440,000, adverse. Check: volume +600,000 and price -440,000 give +160,000, which is the total.

questions.q: Which of these lines needs an explanation under the threshold of 5% or J$100,000?
o: Fuel, J$60,000 over, which is 6.7% over budget
Wages, J$90,000 over, which is 3% over budget
Neither of them, as both are below J$100,000
Both of them, as both are over budget
questions.why: Fuel is 60,000 / 900,000 = 6.7%, above 5%. Wages are 90,000 / 3,000,000 = 3% and under J$100,000, so within the threshold.

questions.q: What was the distributor's closing bank balance?
questions.why: 900,000 + 12,600,000 - 13,900,000 = -400,000, an overdraft. Check: payments exceeded receipts by 1,300,000, which is more than the opening 900,000.

questions.q: What best explains a J$6,000,000 profit alongside a falling bank balance?
o: The profit figure must contain an error, since profit and cash always agree
The profit has already been paid out as a bonus to all the staff
The bank has charged far more interest than the ledger recorded
Customers owe J$3,600,000 more, so profit is not yet collected
questions.why: Receivables rose from J$4,200,000 to J$7,800,000, a rise of J$3,600,000. That income is in profit but not yet in the bank.

questions.q: What share of the J$7,800,000 owed by customers is over 90 days old, and what should the report suggest?
o: 20%; chase these debts and review credit terms
20%; write off the whole amount at once, as lost
12%; stop selling to all of the customers
15%; no action is needed until the year ends
questions.why: 1,560,000 / 7,800,000 = 20%. Old debts need chasing, and credit terms and controls need review. Writing off at once or stopping all sales are over-reactions.

questions.q: Using a 365-day year, about how many days of credit sales are outstanding (receivable days)?
What monthly depreciation charge should be reported for the generator, using straight-line depreciation?
questions.why: 3,600,000 / 6 years = 600,000 a year; 600,000 / 12 = J$50,000 a month. J$600,000 is the yearly figure.

questions.q: By how much does the J$ amount owed to the US supplier change?
questions.why: 12,000 x (161 - 157) = 12,000 x 4 = J$48,000 more, because the J$ buys fewer US dollars. It is a cost to the firm.

questions.q: How should the fire-damaged stock be treated in the report?
o: Left in stock at its cost until the firm is able to sell it
Written down to its sale value, with the loss reported
Moved into next year's figures, to protect this year's profit
Added to the value of the generator, as a new fixed asset
questions.why: Stock that cannot be sold is not worth its cost. It is written down, and the loss is shown in the period. Hiding it overstates profit and assets.

questions.q: Which of these is capital expenditure rather than day-to-day operating spending?
o: Paying the monthly electricity bill for the factory
Buying fuel for the delivery vehicles each week
Repairing a broken window in the office building
questions.why: A van lasts for years and is capitalised and depreciated. The others are consumed or restore the asset to its existing condition and are charged to the period.

questions.q: What is the likely full-year outturn if costs continue at the same steady rate and the licence is added?
How does the forecast compare with the J$38,000,000 budget?
The maintenance planned for month 4 was delayed to month 11. How does this affect the forecast?
o: It is a permanent saving of J$500,000 that can be spent elsewhere
It can be left out of the forecast, because it is not in the actuals
A timing difference; the J$500,000 must stay in the forecast
It cancels the J$600,000 licence, so the forecast does not change
questions.why: Delaying work does not remove the cost; it moves it. The forecast must include the maintenance in month 11 or the outturn will be understated.

questions.q: How should the finance officer keep the forecast useful during the year?
o: Set it once now and leave it unchanged until the year end review
Update it only if the board happens to ask for a new figure
Change it each month without recording any of the reasons
Update it monthly with actuals and known changes, and explain why
questions.why: A forecast is useful only if it is current. Update it monthly and explain what changed, so managers can act on the gap.
